items.title: 6 improvements that make Grafana Assistant better at helping your workflows
items.summary: When you ask Grafana Assistant to build a dashboard or investigate an alert, you're doing so because there's work to be done. To do that work effectively, you need the right data, changes you can inspect, and conclusions supported by evidence. You also want Assistant to avoid mistakes and act quickly.Over the past six months, our team has worked hard to improve what makes those outcomes possible. We’ve changed how agents find context, discover capabilities, edit dashboards, and recover from errors. At the same time, we’ve built better ways to determine whether an improvement actually helps.These projects are closely connected. Better evaluations reveal where an agent struggles. Those findings guide changes to its tools and context. Production telemetry tells us whether those changes worked and where to look next.We've been documenting this work on our engineering blog, Unprompted, taking deep dives into the decisions and implementations that went into those efforts. Today, I want to share how those changes have translated to better outcomes for our users.Dashboarding: faster, prettier, less errorsBy mid-2026, dashboarding mode accounted for 27% of Assistant conversations. Users were also telling us exactly where it needed to work better: some operations were slow, consumed too many tokens, or changed things they should have left alone.The team started by establishing a baseline with Agent Observability and building reproducible tests. Over roughly 10 weeks, the reported dashboarding error rate fell from 2.47% to 0.65%. The 95th-percentile latency for individual operations dropped from 63 seconds to 28.8 seconds, while cost per request fell by 18%.As Dominik Broj describes in his dashboarding write-up, those results came from repeated, specific improvements. Engineers found failures in production, reproduced them as evaluation scenarios, fixed the underlying problems, and checked the results after rollout. The dashboarding test catalog grew from 78 scenarios to nearly 200.Learn more: Read Dominik's blog post, "Our journey to improve Grafana Assistant dashboarding mode"Others build agent loops, we build evaluation loops to get you the best outcomesThat process matters beyond dashboarding. It gives us a way to turn individual reports into improvements that can be tested again whenever the system changes.An AI agent can produce a convincing response even when its underlying work is wrong. A panel might render successfully while showing the wrong aggregation. An investigation might identify a plausible cause without enough evidence. Evaluating the final answer alone misses much of what determines whether the task succeeded.In his blog post about building an evaluation loop for Assistant, Yasir Ekinci explains how we separate the behavior we want from the prompts and code that implement it. Scenarios define realistic tasks and success criteria. Graders examine queries, tool calls, saved state, and conclusions. Repeated runs expose inconsistent behavior, and comparisons track quality alongside cost and latency.That separation gives us room to experiment. We can change a prompt, tool, or model while checking against the same expectations. Coding agents also help inspect failures and propose changes, which go back through the evaluation loop for verification and human review.Learn more: Read Yasir's blog post, "Building an evaluation loop for Grafana Assistant"gcx: teaching your local agent how to designing a CLI built for agentsThis same principle appears in Ward Bekker’s account of designing gcx. Watching agents use our CLI revealed repeated failures: guessing flags, retrying unsuccessful commands, and requesting far more output than they needed.The fixes that came with gcx, our CLI designed specifically for agents, which made the interface more informative. Commands describe their capabilities. Errors explain how to recover. Agents can inspect available fields and filter results before bringing them into context. Knowledge that once required a separate playbook increasingly lives in the tool itself, where it can stay aligned with the implementation.At its core, gcx asks one practical question: what should the interface tell the agent so it can take the next step correctly?Lowering the context burdenThat question becomes more important as the number of capabilities grows. In his post on progressive tool discovery, Cyril Tovena describes how Assistant discovers detailed tool instructions when it needs them. Instead of loading every schema upfront, it starts with compact entry points and retrieves the relevant manual.Across the full registered tool surface measured in the post, initial tool definitions shrank from roughly 54,500 estimated tokens to 504.
